title: Vance Blames Iran War for GOP’s Midterm Losses
author: TIME Staff
body:
Here’s what to know

- Democrats won the House and Senate, flipping key Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Texas.

- Vice President J.D. Vance blamed the Republican Party's heavy midterm losses on the Iran war.

- Speaker Mike Johnson won’t seek re-election as House Republican leader, his team confirmed to TIME.

- Exclusive: Democrats are sending volunteers and lawyers to Mississippi on Wednesday following a closely watched Senate race with a razor-thin margin.

- Democrat lawmakers have hinted at the legal challenges they plan to launch against Trump and his Administration.

The doctors and scientists who won political seats in the midterms

Nov 4, 5:49 PM

The Democratic victors in the midterm elections included people who have spent their careers treating patients, studying viruses, and solving equations. Among the winners: a pediatrician in South Carolina, a microbiologist in Georgia, and a mathematician in Illinois—all bringing experience in health and science to government. Several are joining Congress. One is the next Governor of Ohio.

Working in medicine, in particular, provides an opportunity to connect to voters, says Erik Polyak, executive director of 314 Action, a political organization that recruits and supports Democratic candidates with scientific and medical backgrounds. “You go into the ER and your doctor doesn’t ask what party you are,” he says. Doctors, nurses, and others who work in health care may have heard patients describe their struggles and might have personally fought insurance companies to get treatment covered.

Still, having health credentials alone does not guarantee that someone will craft good policy, cautions Brian Castrucci, an epidemiologist and president and CEO of the de Beaumont Foundation, which works to strengthen public health through funding, training, and research. What matters is how they use their training. “Congress needs people who know how to weigh evidence, ask hard questions, and admit what we do not yet know,” he says.

Read more about some of the health and science professionals who won political seats in the midterms here. — Angela Haupt

Key strategists see voters of color as ‘driving force’ behind Democrats' midterm rout

Nov 4, 5:16 PM

Tuesday’s Blue Wave was powered by voters of color.

That’s a key takeaway strategists in both parties are clocking as they pore through the results. In a memo obtained exclusively by TIME on Wednesday and soon to circulate among the Democratic National Committee’s bigwigs, two of the Democratic Party’s veteran strategists argue that the blowout would not have been possible without that crucial realignment, one that has enormous consequences for 2028’s presidential field.

“Hispanic and Black voters not only turned out at a massive rate, but also swung back towards Democrats in terms of support levels, relative to the 2024 presidential election,” Tom Bonier and Simon Rosenberg wrote in Wednesday’s memo.

Read the full article here. — Philip Elliott

3 demographic shifts that fueled Democrats’ midterm gains

Nov 4, 4:13 PM

Democrats made massive gains with key demographic groups in the 2026 midterms—most notably with young voters, Hispanic voters, and rural voters.

Young people overwhelmingly supported Democratic candidates this election cycle. According to the AP Voter Poll, about 7 in 10 voters ages 18 to 29 said they supported the Democratic candidate in their local House races, while about 3 in 10 said they voted Republican. This follows Trump’s historic gains with young voters in 2024.

“Young people trusted Donald Trump to bring prices down and work on affordability,” Santiago Meyer, the executive director of Voters of Tomorrow, tells TIME. “He betrayed everything that he told us: He made prices higher with tariffs, he did not work on housing, and he started an illegal war.”

Hispanic voters were also instrumental in flipping seats—particularly in Texas, where roughly 6 in 10 Hispanic voters supported Democrat James Talarico for the Senate, compared to just 3 in 10 who supported Trump-endorsed Republican Ken Paxton.

“Key takeaway from last night is that Latinos are the key swing voter,” Stephanie Valencia, a co-founder of Equis Research, tells TIME. “People love to call the Latino vote the ‘sleeping giant,’ but we are the swinging giant.”

Rural voters still favored Republican candidates in 2026, according to the AP Voter Poll, but the demographic shifted significantly to the left: 57% of rural voters opted for the Republican candidate in the House, versus 41% opting for the Democratic candidate. In 2024, nearly 70% of validated voters who described their communities as rural voted for Trump, and 29% voted for Harris.

The rural shift influenced several key battleground states. In Kansas, for example, it helped elect Adam Hamilton to the Senate—the first Democrat sent to the upper chamber from the state in almost 100 years.

Read the full piece here. — Rebecca Schneid

Top Republican campaign chair concedes in stunning defeat

Nov 4, 3:50 PM

Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina, chairman of House Republicans campaign committee, has conceded on Wednesday in an unexpected defeat.

Hudson, who has been serving in Congress since 2013, said in a statement that he has called his Democratic opponent Richard Ojeda to congratulate him and looks forward to ensuring a smooth transition.

“In the words of Ronald Reagan: we lost a skirmish, but the battle goes on,” Hudson added.

Hudson’s loss marks the first time that the Chair of National Republican Congressional Committee has lost to a Democrat in a general election. Trump carried Hudson’s district by about 16 points in the 2024 presidential election. — Philip Wang

Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan launch bids to lead GOP after midterm losses

Nov 4, 2:47 PM

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan have announced that they will seek the top position in the Republican minority in the next Congress after Speaker Mike Johnson said Wednesday morning that he will not run for the position.

“The socialists are coming to Washington with a radical agenda that threatens the America we hold dear. They will stop at nothing to undo the progress we’ve made alongside President Trump over the last two years,” Scalise, who has served as the No. 2 or No. 3 Republican in the House for more than a decade, wrote in a letter to colleagues on Wednesday following the GOP’s sweeping losses in the midterms.

“The House Republican Conference must be the first line of defense in this crucial battle, and we must fight like our way of life depends on it—because it does,” he continued, going on to pitch himself as a leader “ready to lead on day one and chart our path back to the majority.”

Jordan, a hard-line conservative who chairs the House Judiciary Committee, also announced a run for minority leader in a letter to colleagues earlier on Wednesday.

“In these next two years, our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democrat party is—offense, not defense, wins elections. Republican policies prioritize making Americans’ neighborhoods safer, keeping more money in their pockets, and protecting enduring American values and freedoms. To restore our majority, we must restore voters’ faith in our ability to deliver on these principles,” he wrote.

“That,” he continued, “is why I am running to serve as Republican Leader in the 120th Congress.”

Both Scalise and Jordan previously mounted bids for Speaker in 2023, after Kevin McCarthy’s ouster from the position. Scalise beat out Jordan for the internal Republican nomination to lead the conference, but later withdrew his candidacy after failing to secure the votes needed to win the gavel. Johnson went on to be elected to the role following a long and contentious process. — Annika Neklason

Schumer vows to work “with or without” Trump as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress

Nov 4, 12:45 PM

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Wednesday that Democrats are determined to “get the American people’s cost of living down”—a task he said he's willing to do "with or without the President."

When asked how this could work, considering President Donald Trump’s ability to veto congressional legislation, Schumer told reporters: “Just watch.” He did not respond when asked if he plans to impeach Trump.

Schumer is in the running to become the next Senate Majority Leader, after Democrats won 54 Senate seats in the midterms, with two seats still up for grabs as of early Wednesday afternoon.

Trump had previously suggested he would veto Democrat-led bills, but in the wake of the election losses he expressed a willingness “to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country.” He added: “I don’t just want to be sitting there for two years vetoing everything.” —Callum Sutherland.

Vance blames Iran war for GOP’s midterm losses

Nov 4, 12:01 PM

Vice President J.D. Vance blamed the Republican Party's heavy midterm losses on the Iran war, citing the months-long conflict as the reason why some former Trump voters had opted not to support a GOP candidate.

“The reason we lost is the war. The President himself said so last night,” Vance said in a lengthy social media post on Wednesday. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest."

Vance said a conversation with a pollster about pre-election data showed "how a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats."

In addition to the ongoing war, he listed the cost-of-living crisis, calls for an "America first" approach, and the desire for a change in the U.S.-Israel relationship as other concerns among Republican voters.

Vance’s assessment is a stark criticism of the conflict, which is now in its ninth month with no clear end in sight, as recent indirect negotiations with Tehran have yielded no tangible results.

Trump has, for the most part, stood by the war, insisting it will pay off for Americans in the long-run. He told POLITICO on Tuesday: “I am totally convinced that my decision on Iran for the long term good of our country and the world was an absolutely correct one and it continues to be.”

The Iran war is estimated to have cost American taxpayers around $47.1 billion so far. Furthermore, Americans have had to shoulder soaring energy prices as a direct result of the unrest—a point many Democratic candidates mentioned in their campaigns leading up to the midterms. —Callum Sutherland.

Exclusive: Democrats send volunteers, lawyers to Mississippi following close Senate race

Nov 4, 11:19 AM

Democrats are sending volunteers and lawyers to Mississippi on Wednesday following a closely watched Senate race with a razor-thin margin, according to two sources familiar with the situation.

The Magnolia State has become an unlikely battleground for the Senate race, as Democratic candidate and District Attorney Scott Colom is currently leading incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a razor-thin margin, with more than 96% of the votes counted. News organizations have yet to make a projection on the race.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), along with Democratic attorney Marc Elias’ law firm, will be on the ground leading the effort to ensure all lawful votes are counted, according to a DSCC spokesperson.

At least one Democratic Senator, Maria Cantwell of Washington state, is in Mississippi with her Senate staffer in advance of potential litigation arising from the ballot counting process, according to a source familiar with the matter.

The state of Mississippi does not have an automatic recount following the election or a recount request procedure set up. The only way that a recount can be requested is through the court system, where candidates can sue the state’s top election office and ask for a remedy. —Philip Wang

House Speaker Mike Johnson won’t run for minority leader after GOP losses

Nov 4, 10:22 AM

Speaker Mike Johnson has told his staff he will not stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress, his office confirmed to TIME Wednesday morning.

The announcement comes a day after Democrats won control of both the House and Senate.

Johnson, who secured his own re-election in Louisiana's 4th district, had earlier voiced his disappointment over the GOP's losses, but vowed to have a "firewall of House Republicans" standing in the way of Democrats if the next two years become about "retribution."

Johnson has served two terms as House Speaker since he replaced ousted Rep. Kevin McCarthy in 2023.

Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, the current House Minority Leader, is widely expected to take over the gavel when Democrats assume control in January.

In the meantime, Johnson has vowed to “continue pressing forward with our agenda of common sense, and our vision to make America great again” in hopes of the GOP regaining control in 2028. —Olivia-Anne Cleary and Callum Sutherland

How AI Backlash Shaped the 2026 Midterms

Nov 4, 9:41 AM

For the past year, a faction of the AI industry bent on unfettered development looked poised to use its wealth to tip the 2026 midterms in its favor. But on Nov. 3, that accelerationist wing could hardly have had a worse night.

An NBC exit poll found that 56% of voters said that AI and data centers were a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress. Democrats spent more than $100 million on broadcast ads casting their Republican opponents as being overly cozy with Big Tech and data centers—and decisively won in many of those races, including Ohio, Kansas, and Iowa.

Data center bans or moratoriums passed in counties across the country, from Edgewater, Fla., to Bloomington, Ill., while the mayors of Piqua, Ohio and Yukon, Oklahoma were recalled for their previous support of data center projects.

Data center and accelerationist super PACs failed to make a major dent in influencing elections through spending. One of the key candidates they spent money on, Darline Graham, lost to Annie Andrews, who nicknamed Graham “Data Center Darline” and called for a two-year moratorium on new projects. The accelerationists' ineffectiveness opened a pathway for “pro-safety” PACs to outspend them in key races. Several candidates backed by those groups, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Colorado’s Manny Rutinel, won.

The election served as the stunning capstone in a year of mounting anti-AI populism.

Read the full story here. —Andrew R. Chow and Harry Booth

James Talarico says his Texas win sends a message to "corrupt political system"

Nov 4, 9:04 AM

James Talarico's stunning victory in the Texas Senate race was one of the biggest midterm accomplishments for Democrats, marking a significant shift in a state that has not elected a Democratic Senator since 1988.

Speaking on the TODAY show Wednesday morning, Talarico said his win was a clear “message to this corrupt political system” that Texans “are ready for change.”

He went on to frame his victory in the Lone Star State as a call for voters to come together across party lines.

“The real fight in this country is not left versus right; it's top versus bottom, because all of us are getting screwed,” he said. “Last night, the people of Texas sent a crystal clear message that they want change and they expect change.”

Looking ahead, Talarico, who defeated Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton, also vowed to hold the executive branch to task.

“We have to establish checks and balances. We have to hold the executive branch accountable,” he said.

Opening the door for collaboration, Talarico emphasized his willingness to “work with President [Donald] Trump to deliver for working people across Texas and across this country.” —Tiago Ventura

Republican leaders issue defiant response and say they "will not stand idly by"

Nov 4, 8:01 AM

After the expected blue wave turned into more of a tsunami, Republican leaders are reflecting on the results, and making vows for the future, as they prepare for the reality of losing control over both chambers of Congress.

Senate Majority Leader Thune touted what he views to be successful hallmarks of President Donald Trump’s first two years, citing border security and tax hike prevention’s.

Looking ahead to the next two years, Thune insisted that Republicans “will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done” Hailing Trump’s presence in the White House, he said the party will work with the President “to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism,” arguing that “we cannot let their fringe positions become the mainstream.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson was equally defiant in his response to the Democrats’ overwhelming gains. He admitted he was “disappointed” by the results, but vowed to battle on against what he called an “insurgent socialist movement.”

“I’m not going to exaggerate when I tell you that there’s not a single American, not a single American family anywhere, that’s going to be made better off if Democrats turn Congress into a circus,” Johnson said in the early hours. “If they make the next two years about retribution and lawfare and partisan games, every American will suffer by that. And I tell you what we will do. We will put a firewall of House Republicans standing in their way to ensure that doesn’t happen."

Despite the significant setback, Johnson expressed hope for the future of Republicans in the House.

“We will continue pressing forward with our agenda of common sense and our vision to make America great again. And come 2028, we will take back the House, and we will finish this job,” he vowed.

Johnson will likely be handing over his gavel to Hakeem Jeffries, the current House Minority Leader, who heralded the election gains for his party as “not a blue moment,” but rather “a red, white, and blue moment.”

With control of the House secured, Democrats warn Trump Administration to "lawyer up"

Nov 4, 7:05 AM

With their newly-acquired majority, Democrats are prepping to take control of the House committees. This will give them a new subpoena power and the ability to conduct oversight investigations of Trump’s Administration, family and business ventures, immigration enforcement, and more.

California Rep. Robert Garcia, who is set to become the next chair of the Oversight Committee of the House of Representatives, shared a two-word warning for Republicans as the results came in Tuesday night. “Lawyer up,” he said.

The Oversight Committee’s primary function is to hold the federal government to account. It will serve as the core body for lawmakers to mount legal challenges against the Trump Administration.

Garcia previously said that, if Democrats were to win, he would lead investigations into the Trump family’s business dealings, the conduct of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal. He also vowed to look into Elon Musk’s former role in the “Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).”

Elsewhere, the X account belonging to Democrats on the House Homeland Security Committee told Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin to “clear” his calendar.

Homeland Security operations under the Trump Administration have come under fierce condemnation by Democrats, who have raised the alarm over fatal shootings carried out by federal agents in Trump’s second term.

The Trump Administration is also set to face challenges within the Senate now that Democrats have retaken the chamber. Sen. Rob Wyden of Oregon, a ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, hinted at future investigations when he shared a one-word statement overnight, simply saying: “Subpoenas." —Callum Sutherland

Europe hails Democrats’ midterms victory as a rebuke of Trump's policies

Nov 4, 6:23 AM

The Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections are being viewed by some European leaders as a rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Administration’s policies.

“American society voted against the policies that only impoverish. Against hate. Against machismo. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites,” said Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has previously clashed with Trump.

Others viewed the Democrats’ reclaiming of both chambers of Congress as an opportunity to improve U.S.-Europe relations, which have faltered significantly since Trump returned to office, with divides over the Iran war, NATO spending, and tariffs proving especially damaging.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre viewed the results as “a powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters.” In a statement to Reuters, he said that “voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the President and the Administration have stood for,” citing environmental matters and foreign policy as two such examples.

Outside of Europe, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf argued that the results were a reflection of Americans’ rebuke of war. “Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” he said.

The Iran war, which started on Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iranian targets, is currently in its ninth month and remains deeply unpopular with Americans, who have had to shoulder soaring diesel prices and other financial ramifications as a direct result of the conflict. —Tiago Ventura

The results in Texas could reshape the road to the White House in 2028

Nov 4, 5:39 AM

On an Election Day when national Democrats had monumental momentum, the results in Texas were a breed apart and could redefine the path to the White House in 2028.

Both James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa broke the Republican Party’s hold in deep-red Texas. But the losses didn’t stop there. When all the ballots are counted, Texas Republicans may be on the receiving end of something approaching a wipeout. It’s a stunning turn that proves in one fell swoop that years of Democrats’ optimism in someday flipping Texas were not foolhardy. Even Texas Republicans gifted last-minute gerrymandered districts in U.S. House races were not immune to the national mood.

For Democrats, it was a dividend long invested. Year after year, Democrats kept insisting that this would be the cycle that would break the Republican fever in the state. And year after year, they woke up the day after Election Day feeling like Charlie Brown trying to kick Lucy’s football.

Still, Democrats have long insisted that Texas is not a state of Republican voters. It’s a state of non-voters. Tuesday’s results finally proved that thesis.

The shift could have seismic consequences for the 2028 presidential map. Texas has 40 votes in the Electoral College, or roughly 15% of the haul needed to win the White House. If Democrats can sustain their success in Texas, that suddenly means other traditional swing states could prove optional. And both parties may find themselves having to invest heavily in the massive and pricey state to pin down Texas’ electoral votes every four years.

Read the full story here. —Philip Elliott

Nevada AG Aaron Ford beats Republican incumbent to become state's first Black governor

Nov 4, 5:07 AM

Nevada’s Attorney General Aaron Ford, a Democrat, has won the hotly-contested race for governor, defeating Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo to become the state’s first Black governor, the AP called.

With Nevada set to play a pivotal role in the next presidential election, Ford's win is a significant boost for the Democrats.

As the campaign race heated up over the summer, Ford's team criticized Lombardo after police body camera footage showed him dropping his own name during a traffic stop in Las Vegas and avoiding a ticket.

On the eve of the midterm election, Ford honed in on his criticism of Lombardo, linking him to the affordability crisis concerning many Americans.

"Joe Lombardo and Donald Trump have been working together to raise your gas, groceries, housing, and health care costs," he argued, advising people to "vote like your wallet depends on it." —Olivia-Anne Cleary

The midterm historymakers

Nov 4, 4:30 AM

Several election-winners on Tuesday have broken historic identity barriers for the U.S.

New Hampshire Democrat Chris Pappas will be the first openly gay male Senator. Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed will be the first Muslim U.S. Senator. Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan will be the first Native American female Senator. Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Black female governor. New Mexico Democrat Deb Haaland will be the first Native American female governor. And Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, could become the first Black Speaker of the House.

Read the full story here. — Chad de Guzman

Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins battleground Michigan Senate race

Nov 4, 2:40 AM

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat with a background in public health, has defeated Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan’s open Senate race on Tuesday, according to the Associated Press, making him the first Muslim elected to the United States Senate.

The election of El-Sayed, 42, the son of Egyptian immigrants who was born and raised in suburban Detroit, represents a milestone in American politics and a potentially consequential shift within the Democratic Party. An outspoken critic of Israel who has championed an ambitious progressive agenda, he joins a growing contingent of left-wing Democrats who have prevailed in elections this year.

Read the full story here. — Nik Popli

Elon Musk reacts to midterm election results

Nov 4, 2:25 AM

"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time," Elon Musk, the world's richest man, posted on his platform X early Wednesday.

The on-and-off ally of President Donald Trump poured a tremendous amount of money into the Republican effort to retain their congressional majorities: The New York Times previously reported that Musk contributed some $474 million into the midterms, making him the single largest disclosed donor in modern American politics.

In a separate post, Musk, who is the CEO and part-owner of companies Tesla and SpaceX, wrote: "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now." Democrats, who will take control of both chambers of Congress, have made the AI boom and data centers a key campaign issue. — Chad de Guzman

Trump on blue wave: 'I don't view it as a hit on me'

Nov 4, 1:25 AM

The AP has called the House majority for Democrats, having already called the Senate majority for the same party. Moments earlier, President Trump congratulated Democrats on their Election Day success in a phone interview with Fox News, but he went on to say that he didn't think the blue wave was a rebuke of his presidency.

"They did a good job. They’ve been looking for this one for 11 years, and they finally got it," Trump said about Democrats. "But I don’t view it as a hit on me. I think we’ve done ... We’ve had the greatest two years in the history of the presidency.”

This year's midterm election has been described by many politicians and political experts as a referendum on the Trump Administration. About a month before Election Day, Trump's approval rating fell to a historic low of 30%, according to the Pew Research Center. — Chantelle Lee

Incumbent GOP Rep. Max Miller loses amid domestic violence allegations

Nov 4, 1:25 AM

Democrat Brian Poindexter has defeated two-term incumbent Republican Rep. Max Miller, whose campaign was roiled by domestic violence allegations from his ex-wife and former White House Press Secretary Stephanie Grisham, whom he worked and shared a romantic relationship with during Trump's first term. Miller has denied all wrongdoing.

Both Ohio Senators, including Miller's former father-in-law, urged Miller to exit the race. The House Ethics Committee announced in August it was actively reviewing allegations against Miller.

Poindexter, a union worker and local councilman, appealed to working-class voters and centered his campaign around lowering the minimum age to qualify for Medicare, regulating data centers, and limiting funding for the war in Iran. — Connor Greene

GOP Sen. Susan Collins concedes to Democratic challenger

Nov 4, 1:10 AM

Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine in the U.S. Senate for nearly three decades, lost her re-election bid to her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, the AP has called—the latest stunning result in a midterm election that has become a blue wave.

AP reported that Collins conceded the race to Jackson before the news outlet had officially called it. Jackson, a logger and former president of the Maine Senate, posted a victory statement on social media early Wednesday morning, before the race was officially called by AP.

"Maine, I owe you everything," he said. "I’m ready to get to work for Mainers in the U.S. Senate, and I promise you this: I’ll never forget where I came from or who I’m fighting for. Thank you. Let’s go build a government that works for all of us."

A victory by Jackson would not just be remarkable because he's unseating a five-term Senator but also because he entered the race relatively late, after Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary, withdrew from the race in July amid allegations of sexual assault, which he denied. — Chantelle Lee

Read the full story of Jackson's victory here.

All polls have closed

Nov 4, 1:00 AM

All polls in the U.S. have closed. Polls in Alaska and Hawaii were the last to close, at 1 a.m. and midnight EST, respectively. — Connor Greene

Trump rages against blue wave

Nov 4, 12:15 AM

The President railed against Democrats' victories in the midterms on Tuesday evening in a series of Truth Social posts.

Shortly before midnight, Trump posted a photo of a red hat reminiscent of the ones often worn by MAGA supporters and by the President himself—but this one had the word "Veto" printed on it. The image appears to be a threat that the President will use his veto power against the House and the Senate, the latter of which AP called for Democrats on Tuesday evening. AP has not yet called control of the House, but other news outlets have projected that Democrats will win the majority in the lower chamber as well.

In another social media post, Trump levied an attack against Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid to Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday evening—a stunning result in a state that has not elected a Democrat governor since 1990.

Trump had endorsed Abbott in the race. But after Abbott's loss on Tuesday, the President accused the Texas governor of being a "RINO," which stands for "Republican In Name Only."

"If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost," Trump said in a Truth Social post. "He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!"

A few minutes later, the President posted again, saying, "I’m going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!" — Chantelle Lee

Democrats have won the Senate, AP calls

Nov 4, 12:00 AM

AP called the Senate for Democrats shortly before midnight, in a stunning rebuke of the Trump Administration and the Republican Party.

As of Tuesday evening, AP has called 51 seats in the upper chamber for Democrats and 39 for Republicans. AP has yet to call 10 races for the upper chamber. The news outlet hasn’t yet called the House majority for Democrats, but others, including CNN, have projected that Democrats will win control of the lower chamber. Democrats capturing both chambers of Congress would mark only the fifth time since World War II that a political party was able to flip both the Senate and the House in a midterm election. — Chantelle Lee

Read the full story here.

House Democrats celebrate election gains

Nov 3, 11:50 PM

House Democrats are rejoicing over their election victories, including projections from CNN and NBC that they have regained control of the chamber. The AP has not yet called the majority.

In Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ election-night headquarters just south of the Capitol, a crowd of roughly 100 people erupted in cheers when CNN announced the projection. Supporters broke into chants of “Jeffries! Jeffries! Jeffries!”

Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington state, who chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in the headquarters: “The American people have spoken decisively all across the country. They have had enough of the broken promises from house Republicans, and they are ready for new leadership in Congress, and they're going to get it.” — Chad de Guzman with reporting contributed by Nik Popli

Democrat Josh Turek wins key Senate pick-up in Iowa

Nov 3, 11:45 PM

Democratic state representative Josh Turek has been elected as U.S. Senator for Iowa, the AP called, beating Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson to take the seat to be vacated by GOP Sen. Joni Ernst, who is retiring after two terms.

Turek, a paralympian gold medalist, is the first Democrat Iowa has sent to the Senate since Tom Harkin was re-elected in 2008. — Chad de Guzman

House Democratic Leader hails ‘great American comeback’

Nov 3, 11:40 PM

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries hailed a "great American comeback" in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday night after several outlets projected that Democrats had won back the lower chamber.

"America is back...I learned very early on that a setback was nothing more than a setup for a comeback. Today begins the great American comeback," he said. "This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic one. This is not a blue moment or a red moment. It's a red, white, and blue moment because America has won tonight." — Connor Greene

Adam Hamilton becomes first Kansas Democrat elected to Senate in nearly a century

Nov 3, 11:35 PM

For the first time since 1932, voters in Kansas have elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate.

Democrat Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, has won the Senate race, AP called on Tuesday evening, defeating the Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall. Marshall, who had been seeking a second term, had been backed by the President. He is among several GOP Senate candidates, including Sen. Darline Graham, who received Trump's endorsement in this midterm cycle—but were still toppled by their Democratic opponents on Tuesday evening.

Read the full story here. — Chantelle Lee

Texas Governor Greg Abbott loses to Democrat Gina Hinojosa

Nov 3, 11:25 PM

Texas Governor Greg Abbott has been defeated by Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, the AP has called.

Abbott’s stunning defeat marks the end of a long streak of Republican governorship since 1995, including George W. Bush who governed Texas from 1995 to 2000 before becoming President.

Abbott, who has been governor of Texas for three terms, previously spent more than two decades in the Texas judicial system. In 1995, then-Governor Bush appointed Abbott to the Texas Supreme Court. He was then re-elected twice in the late 90s. In 2014, he ran for Texas governor and won by more than 20 points against state senator Wendy Davis. — Philip Wang

Democrat James Talarico flips Texas Senate seat

Nov 3, 11:10 PM

John Cornyn, the outgoing Republican senior Senator for Texas, congratulated Democratic candidate James Talarico, the state representative who defeated GOP nominee Ken Paxton for Cornyn’s seat.

“The voters have spoken, and I want to extend my congratulations to James Talarico on his election to the U.S. Senate,” Cornyn posted on X, before the AP had called the race, though it did less than an hour later. “I look forward to meeting him and offering my assistance with his transition as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate.”

Talarico is the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas since 1994 and is also the first Democrat to be elected Senator by Texans since 1988. — Chad de Guzman

Read the full story here.

What time do polls open across the U.S.?

Nov 3, 3:45 AM

Election Day is underway, and polling precincts are set to open nationwide for in-person voting to add to the more than 58 million early votes already cast for the 2026 midterm elections that will decide the control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency as well as numerous state and local contests.

Polling place hours vary by state, but commonly follow a 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time schedule. The opening schedules of the following states differ (indicated in local times):

- 6 a.m.: Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, some parts of Maine, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, and Virginia.

- 6:30 a.m.: North Carolina, Ohio, and West Virginia.

- 7:30 a.m.: Arkansas

- 8 a.m.: Idaho, though counties may open elections at 7 a.m. local time; parts of Nebraska that are under Central Time

There are also some in-state variations.

- In Kansas, polling places must open by 7 a.m, but state law also allows counties to open polling locations as early as 6 a.m.

- In Maine, polls generally open between 6 and 8 a.m., but towns with fewer than 500 residents may open as late as 10 a.m.

- In Massachusetts, polls may open as early as 5:45 a.m. and no later than 7 a.m.

- While Minnesota polls open at 7 a.m., qualifying small towns may open as late as 10 a.m.

- In Montana, most polling places must open by 7 a.m., but towns with fewer than 400 electors may open as late as 12 p.m.

- In New Hampshire, municipalities decide on poll opening times, as long as it’s before 11 a.m.

- In North Dakota, polling precincts must open by 9 a.m. and no earlier than 7 a.m.

- Polling centers across most of Rhode Island open at 7 a.m., with the exception of New Shoreham Town Hall, where they open at 9 a.m.

- In Tennessee, counties decide what time—between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m.—the polls will open.

- And in Vermont, the polls may open as early as 5 a.m. and as late as 10 a.m.

- Oregon and Washington primarily vote by mail.
